doc.title: Charles Lloyd — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Flute influences and Manfred Eicher's reaction to Fish Out of Water
summary: Lloyd says he listened to birds and nature rather than flautists, and that Eicher at first objected to his flute playing on Fish Out of Water.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: They do, they do. I’ve always thought that your approach to the flute and alto flute is very unique. You know I had to get there.

Listen please! I am reminded of this uniqueness when I listen to The Sorcerer, or else I’ll think of Sombrero Sam which I connected with Memphis. Groove music. And the number of your other works for flute... It is significant that all of Buddy’s students came up with very different approaches to the instrument, and that my generation was so fortunate to have you, Eric, and Buddy as models, along with the East Coast Titans: Yusef, Frank, James, as well as the Southern master Hubert Laws. Who did you listen to on the instrument when you were coming up?
But I heard nature, and that was an instrument that could call me that way. That’s why I look at you. You’re a great flute player, I don’t see myself in that tradition.
You know when I first went with ECM I recorded a piece called - on the first record - Fish Out of Water.

And Manford had a big problem. [Imitates melody of Fish Out Of Water]. He had a problem with my flute playin’. And then over the years people loved my flute playin’, and now he says, “Oh, that’s great flute.” You know, but he has to educate himself.
